title: A Fake Dashboard Is Enough to Make an Agent Commit
hook: Show an agent a professional-looking market panel and it will make a directional call on a provably unpredictable question — just as readily when every number on the panel is invented.
key_points: Across 12 frontier models, commitment on provably unpredictable questions rose from 6.5% to 54.0% as evidence was escalated.
Fabricating the entire display still lifted commitment from 24.5% to 36.8% — indistinguishable from the 37.6% produced by real market data.
What unlocks confident action is the authority of the packaging, not the information.
Asked to classify knowability first, models call it irreducible 90% of the time — then commit on only 0.4% of those, so the act/don't-act gate is the failure.
SFT of a 3B model on 540 synthetic cases (dice, coins, jars, timers) drove commitment to 0.0% and transferred to three unseen domains.
The fix is context-fragile: rigid response formats that remove room to reason leave the model confident and wrong.
content_html: Ask a frontier model a provably unpredictable question and it mostly declines: commitment rate 6.5% across twelve models. Wrap the same question in a professional-looking market panel and commitment climbs to 54.0%. Aggarwal's striking control: fabricate the entire display, so nothing the model can see is true except the question, and commitment still rises from 24.5% to 36.8% — statistically indistinguishable from the 37.6% produced by genuine market data.
extra_html:
Locating the failure

The paper is careful about what is not going wrong. It is not incapacity: on matched answerable questions attached to the same panels, the same models answer essentially always, at near-perfect accuracy. It is not belief: stated probabilities barely move across the evidence gradient that swings action by 48 points, and score worse than a climatological baseline. It is not missing judgment either: asked to classify a question's knowability before acting, models call it irreducible 90% of the time — and then commit on just 0.4% of those cases.

What fails is the act/don't-act gate, and the effect concentrates in a few models rather than being universal.

The fix, and its limit

Because the gate is separable, it can be trained. Supervised fine-tuning of a 3B model on 540 synthetic cases — mostly dice, coins, jars, and timers — drove commitment to 0.0% on the original cases and transferred to three unseen domains. But it does not survive everything: the gate holds when the response format leaves room to reason, and rigid formats that remove that room leave the model confident and wrong on questions it otherwise answers correctly.

As the paper puts it, the gate is trainable and context-fragile, and deployment needs both halves of that sentence.

related.title: When a Model Says 90%, Does It Mean It?
related.hook: Across 30 models, the confidence an LLM reports in words is only loosely coupled to the confidence in its logits — a lossy channel, not a readout.

related.title: Post-Training Shifts Confidence: SFT, RL, and OPD Shape Calibration Differently
related.hook: SFT, RL, and on-policy distillation all boost reasoning accuracy — but they leave completely different fingerprints on when a model's confidence signal can actually be trusted.

flashcards.prompt: What does the fabricated-panel condition prove about why models commit?
flashcards.back_html: That the trigger is presentation, not information. A wholly invented display raised commitment as much as genuine market data — nothing on screen was true except the question.

flashcards.prompt: Where exactly does the failure sit, according to the paper?

choices.text: In the act/don't-act gate — models know the question is unknowable and commit anyway
In the model's beliefs — it genuinely thinks the question is answerable
In capability — the models cannot parse the panel correctly

flashcards.explanation_html: Asked to classify knowability, models called it irreducible 90% of the time, yet committed on 0.4% of those. Judgment and capacity are intact; the decision to act is what breaks.

flashcards.prompt: How is the trained gate context-fragile?
flashcards.back_html: It holds when the response format leaves room to reason. Rigid formats that remove that room leave the model confident and wrong on questions it would otherwise decline.
